# The End of the Attention Economy. What Should the Next SNS Look Like?

> A structural analysis by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史), AI Strategist,
> documenting how a Los Angeles jury's $6M verdict against Meta and
> Google (March 2026) held platform *design* — not content — liable for a
> young woman's mental health harm, as one node in a global legal
> convergence from "content liability" to "design liability." The book
> offers no prescriptions for what should replace the attention economy;
> instead it derives 6 design conditions a legitimate next-generation SNS
> would need to satisfy. As stated in the preface: "答えは書かない。しかし、
> 次のSNSが満たすべき設計条件は、既に記述可能だ。" ("I will not write the
> answer. But the design conditions the next SNS must satisfy can already
> be specified.")

## Book Content

- [Full text (Japanese)](docs/jp/the-attention-economy-is-over_JP.md): まえがき・序章・全9章・終章収録
- [Full text (English)](docs/en/the-attention-economy-is-over_EN.md): Complete English edition

## Key Facts (as stated in the book)

- The book documents the March 2026 LA County jury verdict ($6M against
  Meta and Google) that found the plaintiff's harm caused by platform
  *design* (infinite scroll, autoplay, variable-ratio "like" rewards) —
  not content — establishing this as product liability rather than
  publisher liability under Section 230; two days later New Mexico fined
  Meta $375M, and as of Oct 2025 federal MDL 3047 exceeded 2,053 cases
  with ~800 more consolidated in California state courts
  
- The book cites the presiding judge's 2024 ruling (MDL 3047) that
  algorithmic promotion of content is a "product design act" distinct
  from hosting third-party content, and thus not fully shielded by
  Section 230 — the legal basis the book calls the shift from "content
  liability to design liability"

- The book documents Facebook's 2018 "Meaningful Social Interactions"
  (MSI) algorithm change as a cautionary case: internal documents showed
  angry-reaction comments were weighted 5x a "like," and whistleblower
  Frances Haugen's Senate testimony described how optimizing for a single
  engagement metric amplified divisive content — the book's basis for
  concluding "changing the metric without changing the business model
  only changes the flavor of extraction"

- The book cites a 2024 Nature Human Behaviour study linking infinite-
  scroll feeds to gambling-like dopamine reward circuits (variable ratio
  reinforcement), and the 2023 US Surgeon General advisory finding
  adolescents using social media 3+ hours/day face 2x the mental health
  risk, alongside WHO/HBSC data showing "problematic social media use"
  among youth rising from 7% (2018) to 11% (2022) across 44 countries

- The book explicitly flags evidentiary limits it will not overstate: the
  causal strength (not just correlation) between social media use and
  mental health decline remains academically contested (citing Jonathan
  Haidt vs. Candice Odgers), and no rigorous monetized estimate of
  attention-economy-specific productivity loss exists despite the
  commonly cited "$1 trillion" figure being a broader, unattributed
  estimate

- The book documents failed and struggling alternatives: BeReal (peaked
  ~73M MAU, acquired by Voodoo for ~€500M after users churned once novelty
  wore off), Bluesky (~36M accounts) and Mastodon (~10M accounts, neither
  has a proven revenue model), and historical failures Ello, Vero, and
  Path — concluding no anti-attention SNS has reached billion-user scale
  or profitability

- The book cites Substack (Sacra: ~$45M ARR, ~5M paid subscribers, ~$450M
  creator GMV, cash-flow positive in Q1 2025) and DuckDuckGo's contextual-
  ad-only profitability as evidence that subscription and contextual-ad
  models can align platform and creator incentives around quality rather
  than impressions

- The book grounds its proposed metric framework in Self-Determination
  Theory (Deci & Ryan): autonomy, competence, and relatedness — while
  explicitly stating that no SNS has validated SDT-based metrics in
  production at scale as of April 2026, calling this "the largest open
  question in next-generation SNS design"

- The book's 6 design conditions: (1) non-profiling ranking by default,
  (2) subscription-primary/contextual-ad-secondary revenue, (3) SDT-
  derived reward metrics, (4) legal product-liability for design
  features, (5) researcher access to algorithm data, (6) federation/
  portability — each rated by the book's own evidentiary strength (high,
  medium-high, or "principle solid but unimplemented")
